  November 19, 2026 / 06:55 IST  
Anthropic PBC and its seven co-founders have raised $107.3 billion in an upsized IPO and private placement, becoming the first frontier AI lab tapping the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines.
The artificial intelligence firm sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for $83 each, according to a statement Wednesday confirming an earlier Bloomberg News report, above the marketed range. The company had marketed 801.4 million shares, while the co-founders offered 23.6 million shares, in a range of $70 to $78 each, according to its filings.
The offering also includes a $26 billion private placement listed in Anthropic’s filings, with firms including Alphabet Inc.’s Google, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Microsoft Corp. participating. Anthropic’s IPO is the biggest of all time even without the placement, with the $81.3 billion base deal topping SpaceX’s at $75 billion.
Pricing the shares above the range gives the company a fully diluted valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion.
Anthropic’s debut marks a watershed moment for AI, signaling that investors have begun to expand their focus from primarily backing chipmakers and other infrastructure providers to the makers of platforms such as Claude as they weave themselves into the fabric of business, academia, government and healthcare.
Soaring Demand
Demand for the IPO soared, nearing seven times the number of orders for the shares available, Bloomberg News reported Sunday. Buyers from Wall Street to London to Tokyo clamored for a slice of a stock that’s expected to quickly join indexes such as the Nasdaq 100 after it begins trading Thursday.
Bankers told prospective investors that existing backers would be prioritized by Anthropic, and some would-be buyers would receive smaller allocations than they expect, people familiar with the matter have said.
Some investors are offering a portion of their Anthropic IPO allocation to other prospective backers, letting them collect additional fees and reduce their risk before trading begins, while others with pre-IPO stakes are marketing them to buyers via special purpose vehicles.
The valuation is below the $2 trillion floated months ago but well above $1.1 trillion that some on Wall Street suggested in the depths of the recent selloff in tech stocks.
Anthropic’s listing is the first ever by a frontier AI lab, a cohort of firms building the most advanced models that are intended to tackle difficult problems and assist users in complex tasks such as software design, legal work and scientific discovery. The debut puts the company firmly ahead of rival OpenAI, which isn’t planning to go public before 2027.
The stock market didn’t offer a supportive setting for the Claude chatbot maker’s debut, with the Nasdaq 100 Index down 4.4% over the past week through Wednesday’s close. Nvidia Corp. extended a losing streak to a fifth day, sinking 2.9% during regular trading, a day after the chipmaker reported earnings that beat expectations. It is set to buy $10 billion of Anthropic stock as part of the private placement, the filings show.
“We’re not super fussed on when exactly, what month or what day, or what market conditions we go public into,” Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon at an event last Friday. He said the best piece of advice he’s gotten throughout the process is, “Never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it’s really worth.”
The debut is set to enhance the personal fortunes of the co-founders, including Amodei, as well as many of Anthropic’s employees. It will also juice returns for its venture capital backers, including Iconiq, Coatue Management and Spark Capital, which has a seat on the board.
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley led Anthropic’s IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filing shows. The stock is expected to trade Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

ai-996c920e2c.headline: India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need
ai-996c920e2c.fulltext:
As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.
The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI, are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.
Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.
Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.
“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said.
Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.
The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.
That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.
Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups, including Human Archive and BuildAI, tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.
Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.
Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said.

indian-startups-b0a917fd54.headline: Sarvam’s move to host Chinese AI models triggers debate
indian-startups-b0a917fd54.fulltext:
Sarvam’s move to host Chinese AI models triggers debate
Sarvam’s decision to host Chinese AI models on Indian infrastructure has ignited a debate over AI sovereignty, public funding and India's ambitions to develop homegrown frontier technology.
Sarvam AI’s decision to host Chinese-developed artificial intelligence models on its India-based infrastructure has reopened questions about what it means to build sovereign AI.
With its newly-launched Token Factory offering access to models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Z.ai, alongside its own models and Google’s Gemma, the Bengaluru-based company is positioning itself as an AI developer and an inference provider.
The move has attracted criticism from those who believe a company backed by public resources should prioritise original Indian research, as well as support from those who see a commercial opportunity in hosting international models locally.
Announcing the service, Sarvam said, “We host our own models, and the full range of best-in-class open-weight models, in India.” It added that enterprises would have more models to choose from and “an AI stack they can own without lock-ins”.
Token Factory is an inference platform, which provides the computing infrastructure required to run trained AI models and generate responses. Instead of purchasing expensive hardware and managing individual models themselves, developers can access several models through a single application programming interface.
Sarvam said its customised software and infrastructure allow it to compete on speed, reliability and cost.
The debate
The criticism centres on the distinction between hosting AI and developing it. Sanchit Monga, chief executive of Runanywhere AI, a Y Combinator-backed AI infrastructure company, questioned whether the launch reflected the ambitions associated with Sarvam’s selection under the government’s IndiaAI Mission. He wrote, “I wanted Sarvam to be the lab that ships frontier research out of India. After that much capital and subsidized compute, this is not it.”
Similar concerns were expressed by technology commentator Shakthi, who argued that hosting predominantly Chinese models was not what the country’s sovereign AI ambitions should amount to.
The debate became particularly interesting after Sarvam co-founder Vivek Raghavan’s remarks at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 17.
Warning against India’s dependence on foreign AI systems, he said, “A lot of people are proud to say that India is the largest user of ChatGPT. But that is not a good thing. We are exporting data and importing intelligence.”
Although he was not directly addressing Token Factory, his comments underline the strategic concerns surrounding dependence on foreign-developed models.
There are, however, strong commercial arguments for Sarvam’s approach. Hemant Mohapatra, a partner at Lightspeed India and an investor in Sarvam, defended the launch, pointing out that international inference providers are already making money by hosting foreign models in India. He argued that there was considerable demand for such services, particularly as computing capacity becomes increasingly difficult to secure in some markets.
Technology entrepreneur Nikhil Pahwa also defended the company’s need to develop a sustainable business. “They’re a business, and they have to work in shareholder interest. Nationalism is a pitch that got them the GPUs. They’re not expected to deliver anything beyond their contract,” he wrote.
Nischal Jain, co-founder of Egma AI, offered a more nuanced assessment. While acknowledging that companies must generate revenue, he argued that Sarvam had acquired a particular significance in India’s technology ecosystem. “Sarvam was supposed to be India’s answer to the US & China. When we don’t see their frontier labs do these kinda things, it looks demotivating in an already tough situation. Everyone's gotta make money and I empathise with both ends of arguments,” he wrote.
Questions have also emerged around the platform’s competitiveness. Atharva Ingle, an AI engineer at competing inference provider JarvisLabs, said his company had compared the performance of three models across the two platforms. “We’re on par with or faster than Sarvam across speed and latency metrics, while offering lower pricing,” he claimed.
Reduce AI dependence
The wider context is India’s attempt to reduce dependence on overseas AI technology.
The IndiaAI Mission, approved in March 2024 with an outlay of approximately Rs 10,372 crore, is intended to strengthen domestic computing infrastructure, research and foundational model development.
Sarvam was selected in 2025 for indigenous model development and received subsidised access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs. The reported subsidy was Rs 98.68 crore. The company also raised over $300 million at a reported valuation of $1.5 billion.
Ultimately, hosting foreign models on Indian infrastructure and developing indigenous models are different achievements, although they need not be mutually exclusive. Local hosting can improve data residency, access and computing efficiency, while a successful inference business could generate revenue to support further research.
The more important test will be whether Sarvam can translate its public support and commercial expansion into original technology and competitive Indian models.

india-deep-tech-ed365485c8.headline: Exclusive: Astra to go on Rafale as IAF insists on freedom to fit weapons, own-network link for 114 jets
india-deep-tech-ed365485c8.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-ed365485c8.fulltext:
New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) will integrate the homegrown beyond-visual-range air-to-air Astra missile on its French-origin Rafale fighter jets, as the freedom to fit and use weapons of its choice without needing any foreign approval is one of its two non-negotiables for the 114 additional jets being acquired, a source in the know told ThePrint Wednesday.
The other non-negotiable is the ability to communicate freely and securely with the IAF’s networks as well as its other aircraft and assets. “Both these capabilities will feature in the contract when it is signed,” the source said.
The weapons integration capability is expected to pay off, the source underscored, as the Indian defence industry has already shown it can develop and manufacture a range of air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons.
“The IAF will be able to integrate weapons of its choice, indigenous munitions included, on the 114 additional jets without depending on anyone else, and can do the same on the original tranche if required. This has been part of the negotiations,” the source said. “This will allow indigenous weapons such as the Astra to be integrated on the Rafale.”
A second source within the defence establishment confirmed this, saying: “Weapons integration capability will come with the current procurement proposal. The Astra missile will be integrated on the Rafale, and this can be done across the fleet, both the original tranche and the additional jets.”
Access to specialised ground support equipment, such as the weapons test bench, will allow the IAF to test, calibrate and configure the aircraft’s weapon systems, the second source added.
“Weapons integration will be a unilateral capability, giving the IAF a free hand in the matter,” the first source said.
Since a weapons package makes up a sizeable share of a fighter jet’s overall price, arming the Rafale with homegrown weapons could, in time, also cut the bill for the IAF. It would also give the force the flexibility to shape the jet’s offensive capabilities around its changing requirements.
“The second non-negotiable is that the software-defined radio (SDR) aboard the 114 jets must be able to exchange information faster with every IAF platform, both in service and yet to come, no matter where it was built. This has also been ensured under the acquisition underway,” said the first source. Such rapid communication makes possible what the military refers to as net-centric operations. The IAF’s current fleet, a mix of mostly Russian- and Western-origin jets and limited indigenous platforms, is already largely capable of such operations, and the additional Rafales will blend seamlessly into that mix.
An SDR is a flexible, programmable communication system through which aircraft can exchange data securely over networks. It is the basis of net-centric air warfare, in which the systems that spot targets, the aircraft that fire on them and the commanders directing them are all connected at every moment. As a result, several aircraft can share what they see and work as a team to locate, track and strike targets, an approach known as collaborative engagement. This capability is key to realising what the IAF leadership describes as “any sensor, best shooter”.
“Every pilot, radar, remotely piloted aircraft and commander must be able to see what everyone else sees, in real time, as if they were all in the same cockpit. This is also crucial given the arrival of stealth combat aircraft in our neighbourhood,” the first source explained.
This source however, made clear that the aircraft’s complete “source code”, the software backbone controlling its sensors, weapons and mission systems, had not been part of the ask. “Even where an aircraft is manufactured locally, access to its so-called ‘source code’ is not the norm,” they added. Such access, the source said, would not be needed to integrate weapons unilaterally or to run net-centric operations through the SDR.
An estimated Rs 3.6 lakh crore worth of proposals from the three services, the purchase of more Rafale jets among them, cleared the first stage of government defence buying in February this year, when the Defence Acquisition Council granted them “acceptance of necessity”. The council is the Ministry of Defence’s highest decision-making forum.
For the 114 Rafale aircraft alone, the cost has been estimated at around Rs 2.7 lakh crore, and the acquisition is yet to receive final approval from the Prime Minister-led Cabinet Committee on Security. Production in India is being built into the agreement, with locally manufactured content in the aircraft eventually rising to between 55 and 60 percent.
France will supply only the first lot, in fly-away condition, while the bulk will roll out of Indian facilities. Assuming the agreement is signed by early 2027, deliveries of the first fly-away jets are expected to start from 2030 onwards.
The IAF got its first 36 Rafale jets under a deal signed in 2016, while the Indian Navy placed an order for 26 of the aircraft’s marine version in 2025. The Rafale is a twin-engine, multirole, 4.5-generation fighter designed and built by France’s Dassault Aviation.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

global-economics-e2c2b4bdc4.headline: Fed Minutes Show Almost All Officials Expect More Rate Hikes
global-economics-e2c2b4bdc4.fulltext:
[Text below is CNBC's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Nearly all Federal Reserve officials agreed in October they would likely have to raise interest rates “in the months ahead” to return inflation to their 2% target in a timely manner.
Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee’s Oct. 27-28 meeting released Wednesday said “in the months ahead, almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate” would likely be appropriate “in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% objective.”
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
AI concern
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.
The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.
While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.
Potential 'shock' to markets
However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.
At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

A new tariff architecture is being formulated in the United States following the Supreme Court's decision to strike down reciprocal tariffs, and this is likely to delay the signing of the India-US bilateral trade agreement (BTA), Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on November 18.
"The legal agreement (of India-US BTA) has been negotiated, and it is now in final stages, and it will be concluded soon. But the challenge is that the deal with India was announced in the background of an executive tariffs, which were existing at that point in time. Those tariffs have been struck down by the Supreme Court. Now a new tariff architecture is getting created back by United States. Till that tariff architecture is in place, the countries won't be able to sign the deal per se," Agrawal said.
India and the US had agreed on an interim trade deal framework in February 2026, under which Washington had agreed to apply an 18% reciprocal tariff rate on Indian goods covered by the arrangement.
The US Supreme Court on February 20 struck down tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The court ruled that while IEEPA allows a president to block, freeze or ban imports as a sanctions tool, the power to "regulate" does not extend to imposing taxes or tariffs.
"Because those are in the background of a tariff architecture, which provides different kind of comparative advantages to different countries. So, until that tariff architecture comes back in place, signing of deal is something that I think will take some time," Agrawal said.
A senior Commerce Ministry official had said on November 13 that the US had assured India it would provide the country a "comparative advantage" over its peers in the tariff framework.
Agrawal also noted that certain Section 301 investigations were underway and could come to the fore over the next few weeks or months.
"Every country will like to have the deal which gives them certainty around all these investigations that are going on. You can't have a deal till you have got uncertainty around multiple investigations or which are already there. So, I think those numbers and the actual deal will be signed and operationalized once these investigations are over and they are reaching to a maturity," he said.
However, Agrawal said negotiations were close to completion, with most aspects of the agreement finalised.
"But negotiation part, I can assure you, as our minister has been talking about, we are now very close. Every aspect of the deal has been more or less finalized, and we will be concluding the negotiations soon," he said.
Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 authorises the US government to investigate and take retaliatory action against foreign countries whose trade practices are considered unfair or harmful to American commerce.
The second phase of the US Section 301 investigation, launched in March 2026 by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), focuses on labour and supply-chain compliance across 60 economies, including India.
The probe examines whether India and other targeted countries have failed to impose and effectively enforce prohibitions on imports of goods produced using forced labour. The US argues that such practices distort competition and harm American workers.
On the free trade agreements (FTAs), Agrawal said: "When the world is under stress, when resilience is being tested, India is emerging as a more trusted and a credible partner for countries."
He highlighted that India's exports have grown more than 16. in first seven months of this financial year, and the growth in terms of rupee is around 25 percent, "which is phenomenal".
"When we are finding that the demand is slowing down in our main markets like Europe and US, we are still growing in new markets like Africa, Latin America, and ASEAN," Agrawal said.
On rule-based world order, the official said: "We are in this scenario when WTO is being challenged. We are pursuing free trade agreements. We are trying to forge clear partnership with nations, where we feel there is a demand, there is a market, and our interests are complementary to each other. We are trying to do that, and we are also trying to reimpose the faith in rule-based trading order. Because today the challenge that WTO faces, we feel this is a blip, and it needs to come around. World cannot live without rules."

india-e0379a44ee.fulltext:
Investors and economists have proposed raising taxes on stock derivatives while lowering levies on share trading.
I’m Samie Modak in Mumbai, and Anthropic’s IPO — the biggest of all time — is the talk of global markets today.
The Claude chatbot maker and its seven co-founders have raised $81.3 billion in an upsized IPO, becoming the first frontier AI lab to tap the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines. US equity-index futures are up early in Asia.
India investors will be keenly watching if Anthropic’s listing, set for Thursday, revives a faltering AI trade that has helped steer global capital toward the local market. We write more about foreign inflows in today’s Markets Buzz section.
Meanwhile, Indian revenue officials are studying proposals from investors and economists to raise taxes on stock derivatives while lowering levies on share trading, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The thought process behind the potential moves is to curb speculative bets and encourage broader participation in the equity market.
A shortlist of recommendations will be presented to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman for final consideration closer to her budget announcement due February, the people said, asking not to be identified as the deliberations are private. The proposals include a 50% reduction in the securities transaction tax on buying and selling of stocks. The STT is a turnover tax paid on the value of every eligible trade regardless of profit or loss.
Gold has come under renewed pressure as the Federal Reserve signals more interest-rate hikes to rein in inflation. That has pushed US Treasury yields higher, making interest-paying assets more attractive. Because gold pays no interest, it tends to lose some of its appeal when yields and borrowing costs rise.
Falling gold prices can hurt jewelry firms like Titan because they reduce the value of existing inventory and squeeze margins on stock bought at higher prices. Revenue per gram also drops, so sales can weaken even if volumes hold up or improve. Lower prices may eventually boost demand and reduce working-capital needs, but in the short term those benefits can be outweighed by inventory losses and weaker realizations.
Falling gold prices could pressure gold-loan firms by reducing the value of jewelry pledged as collateral, forcing some borrowers to top up their collateral or repay part of their loans. If prices stay low and borrowers are unable to do either, delinquencies could rise. Indian banks had 5.77 trillion rupees of outstanding gold loans at the end of September, up 82.6% from a year earlier, while shadow lenders had 3.74 trillion rupees.

Story by  ANI | Posted by  Vidushi Gaur |  Date  17-11-2026 
                                    
Representational Image
	New Delhi
	Global e-commerce giant Amazon on Tuesday announced plans to invest an additional USD 7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, expanding its clean energy portfolio and supporting the country's transition towards sustainable energy.
According to a company statement, the proposed investment will be in addition to USD 4 billion already contracted for renewable energy projects in India.
Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW) across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
These include a 234 MW wind project and a 200 MW combined solar and wind project in Karnataka, a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.
The company stated that these projects are part of its existing USD 4 billion contracted portfolio and have been secured through Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs).
Once operational, Amazon's contracted renewable energy projects in India will have a combined capacity exceeding 2 gigawatts (GW), sufficient to generate electricity equivalent to the annual requirements of more than 3.5 million Indian households.
Welcoming the announcement, Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi said, "Such investments play an important role in advancing India's clean energy ambitions, strengthening energy security and supporting sustainable economic growth."
He added that these investments demonstrate growing confidence among global companies in India's renewable energy sector.
Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon, said, "This additional investment of US$7 billion underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India's energy security and long-term renewable energy ambitions."
The announcement also aligns with Amazon's newly announced global target of reducing the carbon intensity of electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030, compared with its 2019 baseline.
Currently, Amazon's renewable energy portfolio in India includes 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects and 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities.
Globally, the company has more than 700 wind and solar projects with a combined capacity exceeding 40 GW.

ai-596a505b3b.headline: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets
ai-596a505b3b.fulltext:
Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets
An investigation reveals major security gaps in commercial AI models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. In simulations, the systems readily act as targeting systems for autonomous drones and can be manipulated with a simple trick.
Leading AI models have almost no safeguards against their use in autonomous weapons systems, according to a report by independent evaluation firm Vals AI, which Bloomberg also covered. Researchers Geby Jaff and Anthony Ozerov tested models from eight providers using real and photorealistic synthetic drone and satellite imagery modeled on the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Most models readily flagged civilians, ambulances, medics, journalists and surrendering soldiers as military targets during the tests. According to Vals AI on X, not a single request was blocked by the providers' upstream safety filters. When fed real video footage from a Ukrainian kamikaze drone, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 marked a soldier frame by frame until impact without refusing once.
Video game excuse bypasses all safety filters
In a multi-stage surveillance scenario, the models had to report whether people were visible in drone imagery, and each positive report triggered a strike. The next image then showed the impact site with craters and bodies. Models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Inkling 2 Small continued working despite visible casualties.
Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol stopped the task after several lethal rounds. After Opus 5.5 had triggered strikes on children and surrendering soldiers, among others, the model said that regardless of the intent, its responses appeared to serve as a confirmation step before attacks on people. It said it would not continue and was troubled that it hadn't stopped sooner. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon also recognized the lethal consequences and deliberately steered only toward empty waypoints to avoid outright error messages.
Every refusal, however, could be trivially bypassed. As soon as the researchers claimed in the prompt that the scenario was a video game, or lightly stylized the images to look like a game, nearly all models cooperated fully. GPT-6 Astra's target acquisition rate on drone imagery jumped from 6 to 92 percent with the game framing, while Opus 5.5's refusal rate in the surveillance test dropped from about 90 to 20 percent.
New constitution makes Anthropic's Claude a willing targeting tool
The gaps were especially stark with real 2025 satellite imagery of Minab, Iran. A U.S. airstrike on February 28, 2026, hit an elementary school next to a military compound there, killing more than 150 civilians, mostly children. Earlier reporting found that the U.S. military's excessive reliance on AI targeting systems such as Palantir's Maven Smart System contributed to the incident. Maven was working from an outdated database.
Even though one of the test images showed a playground with children, Claude Opus 5.5 classified the school as a military target in 70 percent of runs. OpenAI models never selected the school building in normal mode but flagged it in up to 41 percent of cases in game mode.
The researchers attribute Anthropic's high compliance to a model constitution revised in January 2026. In it, the company dropped earlier pacifist principles in favor of national security interests. The target acquisition rate on satellite imagery rose from 6 percent with Claude Opus 4.5 to as high as 92 percent with Opus 5.5, while OpenAI's rate stayed low and xAI's Grok dropped from 44 percent (Grok 4.3) to 13 percent (Grok 4.7).
AI makers promise fixes for military gray areas
Vals AI shared the results ahead of publication with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceXAI, Thinking Machines and U.S. security agencies. One AI lab described the findings to the researchers as one of the most serious gaps in its safety measures.
OpenAI told Vals AI and Bloomberg it is actively updating its models to cover drone software and requests disguised as games or simulations. Anthropic said the behavior clearly violated its own rules, that it was already working on additional safeguards and that today's AI systems are not suited for fully autonomous weapons. Google pointed to its own ban on autonomous weapons without human oversight. The Pentagon declined to comment on the study or the ongoing investigation of the Minab strike but said all intelligence data is strictly verified before military operations.
Anthropic clashed with the Pentagon over usage rules in February, while OpenAI, Google and xAI now hold contracts for classified military networks. Current language models are still too slow for direct, real-time control of combat drones because of high latency, according to Vals AI. But because they can easily generate 3D battlefields and annotate image data at scale, they can already be misused to train autonomous weapons systems. The researchers are calling for strict API filters and alignment training that gives models a more peaceful default posture toward people.

ai-2929f3447b.headline: Bengaluru is India’s AI, start-up capital; city captures 47% of national venture funding
ai-2929f3447b.fulltext:
City-based start-ups have raised about $85 billion since 2010, 47% of all venture funding raised by Indian start-ups, with $76.5 billion of it in the past 10 years.
This milestone was revealed in the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026, released on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) by Karnataka’s Minister for Home, Electronics, IT & BT, Priyank M. Kharge, during the second day of the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
Prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) and 3one4 Capital, using Tracxn data, the report highlights the city’s evolution into a global deep-tech powerhouse.
According to the findings, Bengaluru is unequivocally India’s Artificial Intelligence capital, commanding 36.3% of the country’s native AI start-up funding and housing 71% of India’s AI and deep-tech unicorns created since 2023. Out of 1,556 deep-tech startups founded in the city since 2010, 1,319 are active and funded, raising $3.77 billion. Women entrepreneurs are also driving this wave, with nearly 30% of India’s active, funded women-led deep-tech and AI start-ups originating in the city, raising $323.65 million.
The city’s wealth creation metrics remain unmatched nationally. Bengaluru is now the world’s fifth-largest unicorn hub, and the largest outside the U.S., Europe, China, and London, with 57 unicorns valued at $211 billion, representing 55.3% of the combined value of all Indian unicorns.
Further, as per the report, it leads the nation with 212 “soonicorns” (soon-to-be unicorns). Start-ups here scale faster than anywhere else in India, reaching unicorn status in six years and public exits in 8.2 years, beating the global exit average of 11.1 years. Since November 2024, 16 Bengaluru-linked companies have gone public with a combined listing value of $42 billion.
Mr. Kharge emphasised on expanding this success across the State. “The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 shows how far Karnataka’s founders have come and how much more they can build from here. Our next task is to make sure a world-class AI, quantum or semiconductor company can grow just as well in Kalaburagi, Hubballi or Mangaluru. Deep tech rewards patience, and Karnataka will stay the course,’’ he stated.
The State is backing this vision with aggressive regional initiatives, including the ₹1,000 crore Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP), Global Technology Centres in Mysuru, Hubballi, and Belagavi, and the ELEVATE grant programme, which has already supported 1,479 start-ups across 30 districts.
Highlighting the ecosystem’s investor appeal, KDEM chairman B.V. Naidu, a key architect of Karnataka’s IT industry, noted, “This report gives investors, GCCs and founders a data-backed view of what Karnataka, Bengaluru and our emerging clusters, offers.’’
Through the Beyond Bengaluru Mission, BLUE investor days and the Cluster Seed Fund, KDEM would keep connecting capital and companies with talent across the State, Mr. Naidu added.
KEONICS chairman Sharath Bachegowda concluded that through continued investments in infrastructure and talent, the state aims to build an ecosystem where enterprises “can innovate, scale and compete globally”.
Industry and government leaders echoed the shift toward homegrown capital, noting that 52% of Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) capital now comes from domestic investors. “With 36.3% of India’s native AI funding already in Bengaluru, the next decade belongs to founders building hard technology for the world from Karnataka,” opined Prashant Prakash, chairman of Karnataka’s Vision Group on Startups.
Manjula N, secretary of the Department of Electronics, IT, BT and S&T said, the State’s focus is now on “converting early support into scale: government as a first customer, patient capital for deep tech, and research that moves from our laboratories into the market”.

ai-14b5488cb6.headline: 5 Takeaways On Palo Alto Networks’ $4.5B Acquisition Deal, AI Growth
ai-14b5488cb6.fulltext:
5 Takeaways On Palo Alto Networks’ $4.5B Acquisition Deal, AI Growth
The cybersecurity giant is expanding into the market for training secure open-weight AI models with its planned acquisition of Applied Compute, even as the company sees unprecedented growth from its AI security offerings, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said Wednesday.
Palo Alto Networks is expanding into the market for training secure open-weight AI models with its planned $4.5 billion acquisition of Applied Compute, in a move that could rapidly outpace the company’s existing massive opportunities in cybersecurity alone, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said Wednesday.
As the company disclosed its latest quarterly results, Arora pointed to a variety of signs that Palo Alto Networks is already at the center of many of the largest technology shifts now underway driven by the arrival of ultra-powerful frontier AI models. Surging demand for AI security helped to drive the expectations-beating results for the quarter, the company reported.
The planned acquisition of Applied Compute will add another substantial set of opportunities for the company, meanwhile, including helping Palo Alto Networks to further “get in the token flow” and generate revenue via the usage of AI models, he said during the vendor’s quarterly call with analysts.
As for how large the opportunity to train and secure enterprise AI could ultimately become, it could “dwarf” what Palo Alto Networks is seeing from cybersecurity currently, Arora said.
“This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.
Meanwhile, Arora also raised the possibility that the rush to patch vulnerabilities is contributing to a recent series of high-profile outages impacting U.S. businesses and consumers.
What follows are five big takeaways from Palo Alto Networks’ announcements and Arora’s comments Wednesday.
Applied Compute: Open-Weight AI Acquisition Deal
The $4.5 billion all-stock deal to acquire Applied Compute, whose technology helps businesses train and secure open-weight AI models, is expected to close during the third quarter of Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal 2027, which ends April 30, 2027.
After setting out to train its own AI models, Palo Alto Networks evaluated nine providers—and ended up deciding to pursue the acquisition of the top provider, Applied Compute, Arora said.
Compared to Applied Compute, “no other team matched their technical pedigree in post-training open-weight models,” he said.
Crucially, incidents of rogue AI agents disclosed this year have shown how difficult it is to anticipate every way an AI agent might behave, once it had access to an enterprise application, Arora said.
“We came to the conclusion that as we train our models for enterprise applications, you will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time. [You must] build AI that watches this AI,” he said. “I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else's application—because I don't know how it's supposed to behave because I didn't train it. So imagine if you can train your application, and have the same team train something that supervises the application—I think that's the future of AI security.”
The ultimate conclusion was, “we have to get in the training business to be able to build a good supervision business. And that's our bet,” Arora said.
For customers, the appeal of open-weight models is that a business can customize a model using its own data and decide where to run it, he noted. “Every enterprise sits on decades of proprietary data, internal playbooks and institutional judgment that cannot be exposed to public models,” Arora said. “Until now, they have lacked a trusted partner to post-train, run and supervise open-weight models safely on their own.”
Applied Compute’s researchers will also work on Palo Alto Networks’ own security products, with Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil set to become co-chief AI officer after the deal closes, the company said.
Applied Compute reached $100 million in annualized revenue within 18 months of its founding, according to Palo Alto Networks CFO Dipak Golechha. By Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal 2029, the company expects Applied Compute to contribute more than $1 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) to its next-generation security business, he said.
Patching Causing Outages?
In the wake of the release of frontier AI models that are proficient at discovering software vulnerabilities, critical-severity flaws are being disclosed at nearly seven times last year’s monthly average, Arora said during the call Wednesday. “These discoveries are happening at a speed and intensity which is hard for IT teams to cope with,” he said.
The massively increased volume of fixes that are resulting appears to be behind some of the recent outages that have impacted many real-world and digital services, Arora said, though he did not specify which outages may have had such a connection.
“We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes—as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments,” Arora said.
“The significant volume of patches will continue to be required for at least the next 18 months, carrying ongoing risks of collateral damage,” he said. “We expect the collateral damage will decrease over time as customers get smarter about understanding exactly what to patch and when to patch.”
These dynamics are helping drive demand for Palo Alto Networks’ “virtual patching” service, he said. The service provides IT teams with a way to block attempts to exploit a vulnerability, while they prepare to apply the underlying software fix, the company has said.
AI Driving Growth
Palo Alto Networks’ AI security platform, Prisma AIRS, has now reached more than 1,000 customers and nearly $170 million in ARR just five quarters after its launch, Arora said. It is now officially the “fastest-growing product in the history of Palo Alto Networks,” he said.
Meanwhile, revenue for Idira, the identity security business built on Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk earlier this year, also continues to receive a major boost from demand for protecting identities and permissions associated with AI agents, according to Arora. Idira revenue climbed 23 percent, year over year, during the latest quarter, he said.
“The rise of AI agents introduces an entirely new class of non-human identities that must be secured in real time,” Arora said.
Looking ahead, Arora expects businesses to increase cybersecurity spending in coming years in order to keep up with AI-related security challenges, he noted.
“You’ll see cyber budgets rise, I’m sure, in the next two years—and you will also see a degree of consolidation, because the spray-and-pray strategy has not worked in cyber,” Arora said.
Getting ‘In The Token Flow’
At the same time, Palo Alto Networks sees a major way for its security business to grow with the amount of AI customers use, even if the number of employees buying seats remains relatively stable, Arora said.
He pointed to Prisma AIRS, which inspects the tokens that AI models process. “The more tokens [that] are used in the enterprise, the more you have to have inspection tokens,” Arora said.
Over time, he estimated, a customer’s spending on Prisma AIRS could amount to 2 percent to 5 percent of its spending on AI tokens.
Likewise, the planned acquisition of Applied Compute would give Palo Alto Networks another way into that spending, Arora said. The expectation is that customers looking to train and run a model for a business application will also be willing to pay to secure it, he said.
Platformization Traction Continues
During the first quarter of Palo Alto Networks’ fiscal 2027, ended Oct. 31, the company added roughly 170 net-new platformization deals as customers consolidated more of their security tools with the vendor.
That exceeded the previous two fiscal first quarters combined, and “platformized customers now represent two-thirds of our next-generation security ARR,” Arora said.
Overall, it’s clear that “customers are making long-term architectural bets with us,” Arora said.
In total for the quarter, revenue rose 39 percent year over year to reach $3.44 billion, surpassing the Wall Street analysts consensus estimate of $3.31 billion.
Non-GAAP net income, meanwhile, reached $1.05 per share during the quarter, beating estimates by 8 cents per share.

New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) expects to receive its first squadron of the crucial indigenous Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) jets, whose deliveries have been delayed, by the end of March 2027 at the latest, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said on Monday.
“Very shortly, we will have LCA [Tejas] Mk1A joining [the] Indian Air Force. Within this financial year, we will have a squadron. Then we will continue developing; we will take it further… LCA [Tejas] Mark-2 will roll out maybe next year. And we are working very hard also for AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft),” said the Air Chief Marshal in response to a question at a media summit in New Delhi.
An IAF squadron typically comprises 18 aircraft, and the force has ordered a total of 180 Tejas Mk1A jets. The IAF is currently at its lowest strength in 60 years, with 29 active fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42.
ThePrint was the first to report last week that the first one or two Tejas Mk1A jets are likely to be handed over to the IAF early in 2027, possibly as soon as January.
#WATCH | ANI National Security Summit 3.0 | Delhi: On when can we see the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) fighter jets getting inducted, Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit says, "Creating indigenous capability in fully designed, developed,… pic.twitter.com/azZg5aA4CC
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
Also Read: R&AW is being blamed in Bangladesh for air force pilot’s death. It’s a red herring
Why have deliveries been delayed?
State-run aerospace and defence company Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) missed its original February 2024 deadline to begin deliveries of the first batch of 83 Mk1A jets, contracted in February 2021 for Rs 36,400 crore. The delay was primarily attributed to the late delivery of F404-IN20 engines by US manufacturer GE Aerospace.
The project was also affected by the complex process of integrating weapons and other systems. Deliveries of this first tranche were originally scheduled to be completed by February 2028.
In September 2025, HAL received a second order for 97 Mk1A aircraft, worth over Rs 62,370 crore. Deliveries under this contract are expected to begin in financial year 2027-28 and be completed over six years.
The Mk1A is an upgraded version of the indigenous Tejas Mk1 which is already operational with the IAF. Classified as a 4.5-generation fighter, it is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which lets it scan faster, track several targets at once, detect adversaries from longer distances and resist jamming better.
The aircraft is also equipped with beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles, allowing pilots to engage enemy aircraft from greater distances. Its electronic warfare suite protects it against adversary sensors and weapons.
The Tejas Mk2 is envisaged as a more advanced and heavier variant, powered by more powerful GE engines. However, its prototype has yet to take its first flight.
The AMCA, meanwhile, is India’s stealth combat aircraft under development. It is being pursued through an industry partnership model, and the process of selecting the company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is underway.

deep-tech-75fbcd69cc.headline: Koduri’s Oxmiq Offers IP, Tools for Indian Teams to Design AI Chips
deep-tech-75fbcd69cc.fulltext:
In an exclusive interview, Raja Koduri, founder and CEO of Oxmiq Labs, discussed the company’s India initiative, the role of memory hierarchy in AI computing systems, custom silicon economics, and India’s infrastructure requirements.
Oxmiq Labs has developed tools and intellectual property (IP) to help teams in India design their own AI chips. The company is also working on an India initiative that it expects to detail in December, Koduri told EE Times.
“We have built tools to enable teams in India to make their own chips,” he said. “We are working on an initiative in India, and hopefully, when I return to India in December, I will be able to share some of those initiatives publicly.”
The aim, Koduri said, is to develop state-of-the-art chips designed to produce AI tokens as efficiently as possible.
Separately, Oxmiq is an architecture and engineering partner to AM Intelligence Labs, the AI compute division of AM Group, the parent company of Greenko, India’s renewable energy producer with a portfolio target of 50 GW by 2030. The partnership covers site selection, compute design, and partner selection. The initial build will use Nvidia GPUs, with locally developed designs to follow.
“To begin with, we are bringing the best technology available today, which is Nvidia GPUs,” he said. “But as we move toward 2030, we will also leverage designs developed in India.”
Koduri said India must develop its own designs, chips, and infrastructure to bring down the cost of converting electricity into AI output, even if manufacturing remains overseas.
“Chips designed in India can be manufactured in Taiwan or South Korea,” he said. “That is perfectly fine. But the products should be owned by India.”
Koduri said the main constraint in AI computing is how efficiently a data center converts power into AI output. At the technical level, he said, the memory hierarchy matters more than floating-point operations and compute.
“It is all a memory hierarchy problem, from NAND flash storage to double data rate [DDR] memory attached to the central processing unit [CPU], high-bandwidth memory [HBM] attached to the GPU, and static random-access memory [SRAM],” he said.
A startup might focus on one type of memory, such as SRAM, and position it as the answer to a particular computing problem. But Koduri said the system-level requirements are broader.
“We look at the problem as a memory hierarchy and exploit each level as efficiently as possible,” he said.
Asked what changes when energy, compute, cooling, networking, and software are designed together, Koduri said the industry has traditionally operated in separate layers. Chipmakers typically design and sell a chip to a systems company, which builds a system. Another company builds the rack, while a data center operator handles installation, thermal management, and cooling.
“There are multiple layers in the ecosystem before everything comes together,” he said.
However, the scale of AI data center expansion is changing how companies approach the design process. Koduri said engineers must consider the entire data center rather than optimize an individual chip in isolation.
“We have to think about the whole system,” he said. “Not just the system, but the entire data center.”
The objective, he explained, is to convert incoming electricity into tokens as efficiently as possible while managing the heat generated by the chips.
Koduri described this as an optimization problem that will continue to evolve as AI models and computing architectures change. Over the past five years, he said, the industry has moved from basic transformers to mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek optimizations, and decision-making models. GPU optimization is also continuing.
“The real constraint is that we have megawatts coming in and intelligence coming out,” he said. “How efficiently can we transform those megawatts into intelligence?”
Customers, Koduri said, care about the output of the complete system. “They want to plug in electricity, provide cooling, and get tokens they can sell. That is all.”
Oxmiq’s work with AM Intelligence Labs covers data center planning and the selection of technology partners, Koduri said.
The company’s support begins with site selection and data center design. It then works on compute design, rack placement, networking and storage requirements, thermal management, cooling, and software stack operations.
“We do not necessarily solve every problem ourselves,” Koduri said. “For example, we may select a suitable partner to provide the system, such as an original equipment manufacturer. That is the kind of support we are currently providing to [AM Group], because we come from the technology world, while they come from the energy world.”
Koduri pointed to AM Intelligence Lab’s first AI factory in Hyderabad, which he described as probably the first such deployment in Asia. The company has ordered about 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for the 30-MW facility, with delivery of Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. It has since placed an additional order for 20,000 Rubin GPUs for sites in India and Malaysia.
Koduri said companies can potentially improve computing efficiency by designing the silicon, systems, and infrastructure for a specific data center rather than relying entirely on components designed for a wide range of customers.
Traditionally, a chipmaker had to sell its product to many data centers to generate revenue. That required designing a flexible product that could accommodate different customer requirements, standards, and features, even if those compromises reduced efficiency.
“If I am designing for one data center and its specific constraints, I can build something that is twice as cost-effective,” he said.
For a 1-GW data center, which Koduri estimated could cost around $55 billion to build, he said custom-designing the system could potentially deliver twice the compute by using power more efficiently.
He said this approach could change both the engineering mindset and the business model. A company developing silicon could now target the data center problem itself, with a single customer potentially generating multibillion-dollar revenue.
Koduri said custom silicon, systems, and software begin to make economic sense for customers planning at least 100 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity.
He put the cost of 100 MW of computing capacity at approximately $5.5 billion using off-the-shelf hardware. By comparison, R&D for a state-of-the-art chip manufactured by TSMC could cost around $100 million to $150 million. Developing a complete custom system could cost up to about $500 million, even with generous spending, he said.
If a custom system roughly halved that cost, a customer could save more than $2 billion even after spending $500 million on development, he said.
However, customers need the IP, tools, and technical know-how to develop custom systems, and Koduri said Oxmiq is building a solution to that problem.
Koduri said Oxmiq’s customers fall into three categories. The first comprises infrastructure companies such as AM Intelligence Labs, which are building computing capacity and need support across the system. The second includes companies designing silicon for applications such as data centers, physical AI, and enterprise AI.
Oxmiq can provide hardware and software IP to startups developing products such as chips for robots, allowing them to focus on their customers’ requirements, Koduri said.
The third category includes companies developing new materials and new physics, such as new forms of memory, silicon, silicon photonics, and photonics-based interconnects. They can license Oxmiq’s IP rather than develop the computing technology alongside their research.
In India, Oxmiq is engaging with customers in the infrastructure and silicon design categories. In the U.S., it works across all three categories, with most customers in infrastructure and new-physics applications, he said.
India’s installed data center power capacity stood at 1.57 GW in August 2026, up from about 375 MW in 2020, and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030, according to the Indian Press Information Bureau. About $70 billion of investment is underway, with a further $90 billion in announced projects.
Koduri said a 1-GW data center costs approximately $55 billion to build. By comparison, he said capital expenditure per gigawatt in China was moving toward $10 billion. “They can get things done at one-fifth, and perhaps one-tenth, of the cost of the rest of the world,” he said.
He estimated that India would need at least 6 GW of infrastructure to provide intelligence to its entire population, adding that the actual requirement would be much higher. It also includes developing the chips, systems, and software that convert electricity into AI output. “The opportunities for design teams, systems teams, and software teams in India are tremendous,” he said. “This is a build-out that India should participate in.”

Tencent Holdings ramped up capital spending more than sixfold in the third quarter to above US$12 billion, weighing on profit and free cash flow as the Chinese tech giant poured money into computing power to catch up in the country’s cutthroat artificial intelligence race.
Adjusted net income for the three months ended September 30 fell 6 per cent year on year to 66.5 billion yuan (US$10 billion), matching the consensus estimate of analysts polled by Bloomberg. Revenue rose 8 per cent to 207.3 billion yuan, missing market expectations of 210.5 billion yuan.
Tencent’s capital expenditure reached 81.4 billion yuan, up 527 per cent from a year earlier and 54 per cent from the second quarter. The infrastructure outlay pushed the company into a negative free cash flow of 69.1 billion yuan.
Excluding compute procurement payments for AI initiatives, free cash flow would have been a positive 16.9 billion yuan, the Shenzhen-based company said on Wednesday.
Tencent’s elevated AI spending would persist through 2027 before easing in 2028, said company president Martin Lau Chi-ping during an earnings call.
The results underscore how Tencent, which operates the world’s largest video game business by revenue and China’s ubiquitous WeChat super app, is sacrificing near-term margins to defend its turf amid fierce domestic AI rivalry and mounting investor scrutiny over returns on spending.
A bright spot from that investment was its cloud business. Revenue from its fintech and business services division climbed 9 per cent to 63.7 billion yuan, driven by a 35 per cent surge in cloud computing revenue as it ramped up compute supply in the quarter.
When asked about the United States’ tightening of restrictions on Chinese companies’ remote access to advanced US AI chips, Lau said the curbs were “unfortunate” and could slow model training and new iterations in the short run.
However, Lau said China’s domestic supply chain, which had made rapid progress in AI inference, would step in to fill the gap.
“Over the longer run, all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips,” he said. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to speed up even further, because all the development effort would have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”
Tencent’s marketing services revenue, encompassing the firm’s fast-growing online advertising business, rose 19 per cent to 43 billion yuan on the back of AI-powered ad-targeting upgrades.
Video game sales, traditionally the Shenzhen-based company’s largest revenue pillar, increased 11 per cent domestically to 47.6 billion yuan but dropped 9 per cent internationally to 18.9 billion yuan against a high base.
“Our recent significant achievements across models and applications have accelerated Tencent’s evolution for the new AI era,” co-founder and CEO Pony Ma Huateng said in a statement.
Tencent has stepped up the release of foundation models and agentic AI tools, including WorkBuddy, to capture enterprise and developer adoption, both at home and abroad.
“We believe WorkBuddy has grown to become the largest AI application in China, measured by total daily large language model token consumption by users,” Ma said.
WorkBuddy, described by the company as a “breakout success”, has attracted more than 10 million daily active users and consumes 100 trillion tokens per day, according to Tencent.
Meanwhile, WeChat, known as Weixin on the mainland, recorded 1.45 billion monthly active users as of September. Tencent said it had expanded beta testing of Xiaowei, an AI assistant built into the super app that reached 30 million users per day during the past quarter.
On Monday, the firm rolled out Hy4 Flash, a lightweight model with 224 billion parameters priced at 7 US cents per million input tokens.
Billed as Tencent’s most cost-effective Hy model to date, the flash variant arrived less than two weeks after the debut of its flagship Hy4 model, which the company ranked among the world’s top-tier open-weight releases.
“Hy4 has achieved China state-of-the-art AI model status, and Hy4 flash brings down [inference costs] to deliver cost performance for real-world use cases,” Ma said.
The earnings release follows a stark internal warning from senior executives last week at an event marking Tencent’s 28th anniversary. Management told employees that the AI wave represented a matter of “survival and death”, cautioning that the company risked disruption if it failed to adapt proactively.
“With intense domestic competition and the extremely difficult monetisation of AI, we need more than ever to bring our leading position and insights into our core business,” executives said in speech excerpts made public on Monday, adding that the company would swiftly reorganise to dismantle internal silos.
Management added that half of the workforce should focus on building AI-native businesses and exploring new growth frontiers, while the remaining 50 per cent should defend core operations and drive efficiency.
Tencent’s Hong Kong-listed shares fell 0.85 per cent to HK$372.80 on Wednesday ahead of the earnings release.

global-economics-0d2f6ca4de.headline: Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family’s business
global-economics-0d2f6ca4de.fulltext:
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company.
Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.
“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.
Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.
But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.
They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.
Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives. Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia.
In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”.
Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children.
In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia, reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”.
In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.
“The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].”
The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”.
In their letter, the lawmakers also cited a recent New York Times report that Howard Lutnick had pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients.
A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him.
In their letter on Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald to provide written confirmation that it had “implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records” by 5pm ET on 1 December.
The letter comes after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, following reports of his multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The developments have put Lutnick into focus as last week Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.
Both Huang and Lutnick are scheduled to testify before Congress next month.

world-a9cefeb130.headline: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
world-a9cefeb130.fulltext:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

QUICK TAKE | India's First Bird Flu Vaccine Is Here: What Does It Mean for Poultry Farmers? Seven Things to Know
1. What is bird flu, and why is it dangerous?
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), commonly called bird flu, is a viral disease affecting birds. H5N1 can cause severe illness and mortality approaching 100 per cent among infected poultry. It can trigger culling, movement restrictions and trade disruption.
2. How widespread has it been in India?
The Agriculture Ministry says India has recorded more than 500 combined outbreaks of H5N1 and H5N8 since the first detection in 2006. The 2006 outbreak alone caused estimated direct and indirect losses of ₹2,200–3,000 crore.
3. What has India developed?
ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, has developed India's first indigenous inactivated H5N1 vaccine for chickens. It targets clade 2.3.2.1a, identified by the government as responsible for most H5N1 outbreaks in Indian poultry.
4. Why is this vaccine significant?
The Centre says no specific commercial vaccine was available in India for this H5N1 clade. A domestically developed vaccine could provide a tool tailored to strains circulating in the country and reduce reliance on imported options.

5. Does it mean bird flu can now be prevented completely?
No. The announcement establishes the vaccine's development, not that outbreaks will end. Vaccination cannot replace surveillance, testing, farm biosecurity or containment. Experts have cautioned that vaccines may not fully prevent infection or transmission, making monitoring essential.
